title: The Line
passages:
The Marrow rode the swell like a drunk on a barstool — low, listing, held together by cable ties and prayer. Sol stood at the helm with her bad knee locked and the storm glass clicking in its bracket, each tap a second closer to the season that would eat their mooring whole. Behind her, the tower rose from the gray chop like a tombstone with the name worn off: forty stories of concrete and glass, the top ten still breathing air, the rest drowned in silence.

"Depth line at thirty meters," Wren called from the topside station, fingers dancing over the slate reader. Her voice carried the flat calm of someone who'd watched too many divers forget their own names. "Air mix nominal. Dey, your recorder's green. Don't make me lie to the Factor about why his locker came up empty."

Dey laughed, a sharp bark that didn't reach his eyes. He stood at the gunwale in a pressure suit patched at three shoulders, checking the seal on his rebreather with the easy competence of a man who'd done this a hundred times and planned to do it a hundred more. The indenture brand on his wrist caught the light — a thin white line of scar tissue, seven years bought and paid for, six down and one impossible to go.

"Wouldn't dream of it, Reader," he said. "One big score, right? That's what you told me. One locker, one payout, and I walk off this boat with my name in my own pocket."

"One locker at twenty-eight meters," Sol said without turning. "Not thirty. Not thirty-two. You cross the line, Dey, the money doesn't matter. You won't remember what you paid for it."

"I know the rule, Captain. Thirty meters, memory stays down. Like gravity for the mind." He spat over the side. "My mother told me bedtime stories about the line. So did yours, probably."

Wren snorted. "Your mother didn't have a slate recorder bolted to her chest. Mine neither. That's the difference — we get to see what you lost."

"Then don't look," Dey said. "Let me have the surprise."

He dropped backward off the gunwale with a splash that soaked Sol's boots. The water swallowed him clean — no bubbles, no struggle, just the faint *thrum* of his rebreather fading into the dark. On the reader, his depth counter began to tick: five meters. Ten. Fifteen.

Sol watched the storm glass. The mercury fell another notch.

"Twenty meters," Wren said. "He's coming up on the locker deck. Sol, the Factor's drone pinged us twice already. He wants confirmation on the manifest before storm season locks the harbor."

"Tell him we're working," Sol said. "Tell him the Marrow delivers. Always."

"Even when the cargo's a ghost?"

"Especially then."

At twenty-seven meters, Dey's voice cracked over the comm — steady, professional, describing a sealed locker with a corporate stamp Sol couldn't read from here. *Matsuo-Klein Biologics. Cold-chain intact. This one's worth berths, Captain. Real berths. High ground.*

The counter hit twenty-eight.

Twenty-nine.

"Dey," Wren said. Her fingers froze on the reader. "Depth line. Come up."

Static. Then Dey's voice again, lighter now, edged with something that wasn't humor: *Almost there. Just a little deeper. The lock's jammed — need to work the manual override. Won't take a minute.*

"Dey Okafor," Sol said, her hand closing on the rail until the knuckles whitened. "You cross that line, I'm not diving for you. Not this season. Not ever."

*Copy that, Captain. Just — *

The comm cut. The depth counter kept climbing: thirty. Thirty-one. Thirty-two.

On the reader, Dey's heart rate spiked. His oxygen sat steady. But the slate recorder — the black box bolted to every diver's chest that wrote their hours in code no human could read — began to blink red.

Wren went pale. "He's past the line. He's *past* it, and his slate's still recording."

"Meaning?"

"Meaning whatever he's doing down there, he'll never remember it. And neither will we — unless I rebuild it from the slate when he surfaces." She met Sol's eyes. "If he surfaces."

The storm glass clicked again. Thirty-three meters on the counter, and something in the tower's drowned floors groaned — a sound like a bone breaking under pressure, carried up through water and steel to rattle in the Marrow's hull.

Sol didn't blink. "Winch ready?"

"Always."

"Then we wait. And if he doesn't come up on his own — " She left it there, the threat and the promise tangled together like the cables holding the boat afloat.

On the reader, the depth counter hit thirty-five meters and kept falling.

For a long moment the two of them just watched the counter fall, because watching was all the plan they had. Thirty-six. Thirty-seven. The slate's red eye wrote on.

"Pull him," Sol said finally. "Three tugs on the tether, the winch brings him up whether he likes it or not."

Wren's hand hovered over the tether control, a worn brass toggle that would haul a diver topside faster than any man could swim against. "He's past thirty-five. If I yank him now he comes up too fast, gas in his blood like fizz in a dropped bottle. He'll bend."

"Then yank him slow."

"There's no slow. There's the winch speed or his speed, and his speed is down." She keyed the comm anyway, voice pitched hard enough to cut through water. "Dey Okafor. Tug your tether. Two taps. Let me know you're mine and not the tower's."

For a moment there was nothing but the rebreather — the machine that stripped the carbon dioxide out of each breath and fed the rest back, the reason he wasn't trailing bubbles to the surface. Its rhythm had gone slow and even. Too even. A diver fighting a jammed lock should sound like a man swearing, not a man settling in for the night.

"Air?" Sol asked.

Wren checked the second counter. "He loaded a forty-minute bottom mix. He's used nineteen."

"So he's got twenty."

"He's got twenty he can trust. Below the line the mix does things. He starts breathing like that—" she nodded at the slow, patient rhythm in the comm— "and I don't know if the twenty is real or if he's coasting on the last good decision he made."

Sol looked at the storm glass. The mercury had dropped a full line since Dey went over, faster than the season had any right to fall, and she didn't say so, because saying so made it true. "Keep talking to him. If he answers, he's still up there somewhere."

Wren talked. She talked about the payout, the berths, the seven years he'd bled to buy and the one he had left, the name he wanted back in his own pocket. She talked the way you talk to a sleepwalker on a ledge, warm and steady and pretending you weren't scared. The slate blinked its red eye the whole time, writing down every second he'd never get back.

Thirty-eight.

Then the tower groaned again, deep and long, and a shiver of silt rolled up the comm as a hiss — the sound of a floor somewhere shifting off its moorings, concrete letting go of what it had held for twenty years.

The comm crackled.

"Dey?" Wren's voice jumped an octave. "Dey, key up. Say the lock. Say anything."

His voice came back — but wrong.

"Cold-chain intact," Dey said, bright and easy, exactly the way he'd sounded at twenty-eight meters. "This one's worth berths, Captain. Real berths."

"Copy that," Sol said slowly. "You've got the locker?"

"Cold-chain intact," Dey said. "This one's worth berths. Real berths."

Wren went still. That wasn't a man on a comm. That was a recording of a man, the same eight words in the same bright order, the smile still in them though his mouth was forty meters down in the dark doing something else entirely.

"Dey," she said. "What's the manual override look like? Describe it to me. Right now. New words."

A pause, long enough to hurt.

"Cold-chain intact," Dey said, for the third time, and this time there was a hitch in it, a stutter, like the words were skipping against a groove worn too deep. "Real — real — real berths. Won't take a minute. Just a little deeper."

Sol's hand was on the winch before Wren could stop her.
